senses.gloss:
savicāra-samāpatti
------------------------------------------
The Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) has used the word सṁयम as a technical term (vide 3.4). It denotes धारणा (fixing the मिन्द् on an object), ध्यान (meditation) and समाधि (total absorption) on the same object of concentration.
When सṁयम on a gross object leads to its realisation, revealing everything about it, it is called savitarka-समापत्ति (or समाधि). When this realisation—after practice—comes instantaneously without the intervening processes of details involved in the meditation, it is called nirvitarka-समापत्ति.
When the मिन्द् is raised from the gross to the subtle aspects of the same object like the five तन्मात्रस् up to प्रकृति, the समाधि is known as सविचार-समापत्ति.
The yogic power generated by the first leads to the next step; as for instance, from the savitarka to the nirvitarka and from the savicāra to the nirvicāra (ibid 1.17; 1.44).
See also NIRVICĀRASAMĀPATTI.

sāvitrīpraveśa
(‘entering into the सावित्री [Gāyatrī] मन्त्र’)
------------------------------------------
Most of the धर्मशास्त्रस् have ruled that सṁन्यास (monastic life) is permitted only to the ब्राह्मणस्.
A ब्राह्मण householder is expected to keep the śikhā (tuft of hair) and the यज्ञोपवीत (the sacred thread) which alone make him eligible for the performance of Vedic and other rituals.
However, when he wishes to embrace सṁन्यास, he will have to give up all the ritualistic actions of the previous stages of life. This includes the giving up the śikhā, the यज्ञोपवीत as also the सन्ध्या ritual along with the गायत्री (= सावित्री) मन्त्र.
The सावित्रीप्रवेश is one of the steps in this process, wherein the सावित्री (Gāyatrī) मन्त्र is internalised. This is done by repeating the ओङ्कार, the व्याहृतिस् and the सावित्री मन्त्र thus:
Om bhūḥ, sāvitrīm praviśāmi,
tat saviturvareṇyam;
Om bhuvaḥ, sāvitrīm praviśāmi,
bhargo devasya dhīmahi;
Oṁ svaḥ, sāvitrīm praviśāmi,
dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt;
Om bhūrbhuvassuvaḥ sāvitrīm praviśāmi,
tatsaviturvareṇyam bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt ॥

Śavasādhanā
(‘a [tāntrik] practice involving a dead-body’)
------------------------------------------
Certain tāntrik works like the Kaulāvalīnirṇaya (14.75-260) describe this terrible sādhanā involving a corpse whereby the aspirant can get what he wants, in a single night.
He has to get the corpse of a man as per the instructions given in the works, wash it first, offer worship to it and then to दुर्गा or Kālī at dead of night in a cemetery. He has to repeat the prescribed मन्त्र. If he is not frightened by the terrific sights and experiences, and after following a long procedure he secures the fulfilment of his desires.

Sāvitrī
------------------------------------------
Along with सीता and दमयन्ती, सावित्री also has been considered a paragon of wifely virtues. Her story appears in detail in the Mahābhārata (Vanaparva, chapters 293-299).
She was the daughter of the king अश्वपति of Madradeśa. She chose to marry सत्यवान्, the only son of the blind king द्युमत्सेन of Sālvadeśa, even though the sage नारद had warned her that he would die just after a year.
Dyumatsena was living with his wife in a hermitage in a forest after being deposed by the enemies. सत्यवान् was living with them, serving them with great care and devotion.
On that fateful day, सावित्री insisted upon accompanying सत्यवान् to the forest for his normal work. When, after some work, he fell sick and lay down on her lap, god यम appeared there with his noose to take सत्यवान्’s सोउल् to his world. Because of her power of chastity, she was able, not only to see him but also follow him! After much argument—in spite of यम’s persuasive efforts to send her back—she so pleased him with her devotion to her husband that he revived सत्यवान्, gave him a long life as also other boons she asked for. As a result, द्युमत्सेन regained his eyesight and kingdom. सत्यवान् became the king in course of time.
See also GĀYATRĪ.

savikalpaka
(‘with details’)
------------------------------------------
This word has two applications. In pratyakṣapramāṇa (direct perception) it refers to a perception with all the details. For instance, when we see a pot and note its general presence, it is निर्विकल्पक perception (‘Here is a pot.’). But, when we closely observe its size, colour, position and other details it becomes सविकल्पक perception (‘This is a small black pot kept on a table.’).
As applied to समाधि, it refers to samprajñātasamādhi, wherein all the details of the object of meditation are seen and known very clearly.
See also ASAMPRAJÑĀTA and NIRVIKALPAKA.

savyabhicāra
(‘irregular middle’)
------------------------------------------
According to the न्याय system of Hindu philosophy, there are five kinds of hetvābhāsas (invalid reasonings) of which the first is सव्यभिचार. Here the middle term of the syllogism is irregular.
To illustrate:
All bipeds are rational.
Swans are bipeds.
Hence, swans are rational.
Since the middle term ‘biped’ is not uniformly related to the major term ‘rational,’ the conclusion is wrong.
(Vyabhicāra is a technical term which means the absence of cause and effect relationship between two things.)
See also HETVĀBHĀSA.

savana
(‘to press out’)
------------------------------------------
The process of pressing the सोम stalks to prepare the सोम juice for offering as oblations in a सोमयाग is known as सवन. The day on which it is done is called sutyā.
The pressing is done three times during this day: in the morning, at noon and in the afternoon. They are respectively called prātassavana, mādhyandinasavana and tṛtīyasavana.
They all follow the same pattern.
These three savanas are referred to even in the Ṛgveda (3.28.1, 4 and 5) thereby showing that this rite of सवन is quite ancient.
